[1, 6, 7] The event, themed "CONNECTIONS", brought together researchers and clinicians to explore the latest developments in evidence-based obesity science. [2] The program covered a wide spectrum of topics, including cutting-edge basic and clinical research, state-of-the-art treatment and prevention strategies, and public policy. [3, 4, 6] Pre-conference courses and other associated events took place starting October 13. [2, 5] <2> A research paper published in a peer-reviewed journal on October 2, 2023, provided an update on the global obesity epidemic. The paper suggests that there are indications of a potential flattening or stabilization in the rate of increasing obesity among adults in some high-income countries after the decade of 2000-2010. [19] Despite this possible plateau, the authors emphasize that the overall prevalence of obesity remains at unacceptably high levels globally. [19] They also caution that there is no guarantee this stabilization will be maintained, and the burden of major health problems associated with obesity continues to rise worldwide. [19] <3> A prospective cohort study published in The BMJ on September 27, 2023, reinforces the importance of carbohydrate quality for long-term weight management. The study analyzed data from 136,432 US health professionals over periods of up to 28 years and found that, on average, participants gained 1.5 kg every four years. Increased consumption of carbohydrates from sources like whole grains, fruit, and non-starchy vegetables was associated with less weight gain. Specifically, a 100g/day increase from whole grains was linked to 0.4 kg less gain, fruit to 1.6 kg less gain, and non-starchy vegetables to 3.0 kg less gain. Conversely, increased intake of refined grains and starchy vegetables (like peas, corn, and potatoes) was associated with more weight gain, at rates of 0.8 kg and 2.6 kg respectively per 100g/day increase. The associations were observed to be stronger among participants who already had excessive body weight. The findings suggest that limiting added sugars, sugar-sweetened beverages, refined grains, and starchy vegetables in favor of higher quality carbohydrate sources may support weight control efforts. <4> On September 21, 2023, Trust for America's Health (TFAH) released its 20th annual report, "State of Obesity 2023: Better Policies for a Healthier America". The analysis, which utilized 2022 data from the CDC's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, revealed that 22 states had an adult obesity prevalence of 35 percent or higher. This was an increase from 19 states that met this threshold in the prior year's report. A decade prior, no state had an adult obesity rate at or above the 35 percent level. <5> A large prospective cohort study, NutriNet-Santé, published in The BMJ, investigated the link between food additive emulsifiers and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in 95,442 French adults. The study, which followed participants for a median of 7.4 years, found positive associations between a higher intake of certain emulsifiers and an increased risk of overall cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease. Specifically, higher consumption of celluloses (E460, E466), and certain monoglycerides and diglycerides of fatty acids (E472b, E472c) were linked to a greater risk of CVD. The study highlights that emulsifiers are among the most common additives in ultra-processed foods, which constitute 30-60% of the dietary energy intake in Europe and North America and have been previously associated with obesity and other chronic diseases. While the study is observational and cannot establish causality, its findings suggest a potential mechanism for diet-related health risks and support the need for further research on the long-term effects of these common food additives. <6> In an announcement on August 28, 2023, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (ODPHP) designated September 2023 as National Childhood Obesity Awareness Month. This initiative was part of their monthly recognition of National Health Observances (NHOs) aimed at improving health across the nation. To support the campaign, ODPHP provided a variety of resources to help organizations and individuals spread awareness. These included materials for parents from MyHealthfinder on helping children maintain a healthy weight and making nutritious snack choices. The observance addresses the fact that approximately one in five U.S. children is affected by obesity, which can lead to health issues like type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. <7> A KFF Health Tracking Poll published in August 2023 revealed that a significant majority of U.S. adults (80%) believe health insurance companies should cover the cost of new prescription weight loss drugs for individuals diagnosed as overweight or obese. This support is widespread across partisan lines, with 88% of Democrats, 81% of independents, and 77% of Republicans in favor. However, public support is halved when faced with the possibility of increased costs for everyone; only 50% would continue to support coverage if it meant a rise in monthly insurance premiums. The poll, which surveyed 1,327 adults, was conducted from July 11-19, 2023. <8> A retrospective study published in the European Journal of Psychotraumatology on July 18, 2023, examined the link between weight status and mental health in 16,184 European adults aged 50 and over. [1] The study, which analyzed data from waves 4 (2010) and 8 (2019/20) of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), found a unidirectional relationship where Body Mass Index (BMI) was a significant predictor of depression and quality of life. [1, 2] Specifically, individuals with obesity, as well as those who were overweight or underweight, showed significantly lower quality of life and higher depression scores over a 10-year period compared to those of normal weight, with the effect being most pronounced in those with obesity. [1, 3] However, the study did not find a reciprocal association, meaning that depression and quality of life did not significantly predict BMI in the long term. [2, 3] The authors concluded that while there is a clear one-way effect of BMI on mental health, further research is needed to explore the complexities of this relationship. [1, 2] <9> Detailed results from Eli Lilly's SURMOUNT-2 phase 3 clinical trial for tirzepatide were presented at the American Diabetes Association's (ADA) 83rd Scientific Sessions, which took place from June 23-26, 2023, and were simultaneously published in The Lancet on June 24, 2023. [7, 10, 11] The presentation and publication confirmed the drug's effectiveness, reinforcing topline results announced in April 2023. [8] The study showed that tirzepatide led to a superior and clinically meaningful mean weight reduction of up to 15.7% (34.4 lbs or 15.6 kg) at the 15 mg dose compared to placebo in adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On March 8, 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded the approval for Wegovy (semaglutide) injection. The new indication is to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death, heart attack, and stroke in adults with known cardiovascular disease who are also overweight or have obesity. This approval makes Wegovy the first weight-loss medication authorized to prevent life-threatening cardiovascular events in this specific patient group. The decision was based on the SELECT clinical trial, a study involving over 17,600 participants, which demonstrated that Wegovy significantly lowered the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events to 6.5% compared to 8% in the placebo group. The treatment should be used as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. <2> The 10th annual Obesity Care Week, a five-day public awareness campaign, was held from March 4 to March 8, 2024, with the first day coinciding with World Obesity Day. [1, 5] Supported by over 130 health organizations, the campaign aimed to change societal views on obesity by promoting the understanding that it is a complex, chronic disease driven by biology, not a lack of willpower. [1, 3] The week focused on advocating for access to science-based treatments and providing educational resources for patients, healthcare professionals, and the public. [4] A key component of the 2024 activities included advocates returning to Capitol Hill to lobby for the Treat and Reduce Obesity Act. The resolution's title explicitly links its introduction to World Obesity Day, which is observed annually on March 4. This timing was a deliberate effort to draw political attention to what the sponsors describe as a public health crisis, particularly within underserved communities. The resolution supports the need to establish a comprehensive care framework for the over 42% of adults and 19% of children and adolescents in the U.S. living with obesity. [2, 3] After 13 weeks, patients receiving weekly doses of VK2735 showed a statistically significant mean body weight reduction of up to 14.7% from baseline, and up to 13.1% when compared with a placebo. [1, 4] Furthermore, up to 88% of patients in the treatment groups achieved 10% or more body weight loss, compared to just 4% in the placebo group. [4] Researchers noted that the weight loss was progressive and showed no signs of plateauing at the 13-week mark, suggesting potential for further reduction with extended dosing. [3] The treatment also demonstrated an encouraging safety and tolerability profile, with most adverse events being mild or moderate. [2] <5> Spearheaded by the National Consumers League (NCL) and the National Council on Aging (NCOA), the 'Obesity Bill of Rights' for older adults was developed over the course of a year. The process involved extensive research and a series of four town hall meetings in California, Delaware, Mississippi, and Oklahoma between June and August 2023, where over 250 older adults and community leaders provided input. Following the town halls, a preliminary draft was created. This draft was then reviewed and discussed by leading obesity experts during a roundtable event hosted at The Obesity Society's annual meeting (ObesityWeek®) in October 2023. After incorporating further feedback from specialists in minority, aging, and rural health, the final 'Obesity Bill of Rights' was publicly announced on January 31, 2024. This initiative, developed after a year of consultation with obesity specialists and community feedback, established eight fundamental rights for patients to improve obesity care. The launch was supported by an initial coalition of nearly 40 national obesity and chronic disease organizations, . The bill of rights aims to ensure individuals are treated with respect, have access to qualified health providers and treatment, and receive insurance coverage, addressing systemic weight bias and ageism. Concurrent with the launch, a new grassroots movement called Right2ObesityCare was introduced to help advance the necessary changes in federal, state, and employer policies to see the rights incorporated into standard medical practice. <7> On January 25, 2024, the Obesity Action Coalition (OAC) publicly expressed concern regarding a Virginia budget proposal to limit Medicaid coverage of anti-obesity medications to individuals with a Body Mass Index (BMI) of 40 or higher. [2] The OAC argued that this restriction contravenes standard clinical guidelines. [3] <8> Eli Lilly and Company launched LillyDirect on January 4, 2024, a direct-to-consumer digital healthcare platform for patients in the U.S. managing obesity, migraines, or diabetes. [1, 3, 4] The service provides an end-to-end patient experience, offering disease management resources, tailored support, and access to independent telehealth providers like Form Health to determine medical necessity for prescriptions. [1, 2, 4] LillyDirect also facilitates direct-to-your-door home delivery of select Eli Lilly medications, such as the weight-loss drug Zepbound, through third-party pharmacy services. [1, 2] The stated goal of the platform is to simplify the healthcare process and improve accessibility for patients, including those in underserved or rural communities. [3, 4] <9> On January 4, 2024, the Obesity Action Coalition (OAC) announced it had submitted comments supporting a proposed regulatory change in Alabama to update Medicaid coverage for anti-obesity medications. [2] This action was part of a series of policy comments the OAC made in early 2024 to various states, including Maryland, California, Kentucky, and Virginia, advocating for better access to evidence-based obesity care. [2]

The request urged the administration to provide Medicare coverage for comprehensive obesity care. This included two key asks: expanding Medicare Part B coverage for intensive behavioral therapy (IBT) by broadening the types of qualified providers and programs, and providing Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage for FDA-approved anti-obesity medications. The letter highlighted that current CMS policy prohibits Part D coverage for these medications based on an outdated federal statute. <2> On May 20, 2024, the Obesity Action Coalition (OAC) announced its support for New York State legislation aimed at improving access to comprehensive obesity care. [3] The OAC submitted comments backing bills S.8959 and A.8045, which propose that Medicaid and other state-sponsored and commercial health plans cover a wide range of obesity treatments. [7, 12] These treatments include prevention and wellness programs, nutrition counseling, intensive behavioral therapy, bariatric surgery, and FDA-approved anti-obesity medications. [6, 12] The proposed legislation stipulates that coverage criteria for these medications should not be more restrictive than FDA-approved indications and that obesity care should be on par with coverage for other diseases. [6, 12] This legislative effort addresses the high prevalence of obesity in New York, where over 30% of residents are affected by obesity and another 33% by overweight, by aiming to provide more equitable access to necessary medical treatments. [7] <3> On March 8, 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded the approval for Wegovy (semaglutide) injection. The new indication is to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death, heart attack, and stroke in adults with known cardiovascular disease who are also overweight or have obesity. This approval makes Wegovy the first weight-loss medication authorized to prevent life-threatening cardiovascular events in this specific patient group. The decision was based on the SELECT clinical trial, a study involving over 17,600 participants, which demonstrated that Wegovy significantly lowered the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events to 6.5% compared to 8% in the placebo group. [1, 3] The week focused on advocating for access to science-based treatments and providing educational resources for patients, healthcare professionals, and the public. [4] A key component of the 2024 activities included advocates returning to Capitol Hill to lobby for the Treat and Reduce Obesity Act. The resolution's title explicitly links its introduction to World Obesity Day, which is observed annually on March 4. This timing was a deliberate effort to draw political attention to what the sponsors describe as a public health crisis, particularly within underserved communities. The resolution supports the need to establish a comprehensive care framework for the over 42% of adults and 19% of children and adolescents in the U.S. living with obesity. [1, 4] Furthermore, up to 88% of patients in the treatment groups achieved 10% or more body weight loss, compared to just 4% in the placebo group. [4] Researchers noted that the weight loss was progressive and showed no signs of plateauing at the 13-week mark, suggesting potential for further reduction with extended dosing. [3] The treatment also demonstrated an encouraging safety and tolerability profile, with most adverse events being mild or moderate. [1, 3] Their proposed framework advocates for increasing access to effective treatments, including reducing barriers to anti-obesity medications, intensive behavioral therapy, nutritional counseling, and bariatric surgery. [1, 3] Furthermore, the article emphasizes that combating weight-related stigma, particularly from physicians, must be a central part of any effective obesity care agenda to ensure continuity of care and build patient-clinician trust. Following the town halls, a preliminary draft was created. This draft was then reviewed and discussed by leading obesity experts during a roundtable event hosted at The Obesity Society's annual meeting (ObesityWeek®) in October 2023. After incorporating further feedback from specialists in minority, aging, and rural health, the final 'Obesity Bill of Rights' was publicly announced on January 31, 2024. The initiative, endorsed by nearly 40 organizations at its launch, establishes eight essential rights to ensure people with obesity are properly screened, diagnosed, counseled, and treated according to medical guidelines, without facing weight bias or ageism. <9> The National Consumers League (NCL) and the National Council on Aging (NCOA) launched the nation's first 'Obesity Bill of Rights' on January 31, 2024. This initiative, developed after a year of consultation with obesity specialists and community feedback, established eight fundamental rights for patients to improve obesity care. The launch was supported by an initial coalition of nearly 40 national obesity and chronic disease organizations, . The bill of rights aims to ensure individuals are treated with respect, have access to qualified health providers and treatment, and receive insurance coverage, addressing systemic weight bias and ageism. Concurrent with the launch, a new grassroots movement called Right2ObesityCare was introduced to help advance the necessary changes in federal, state, and employer policies to see the rights incorporated into standard medical practice. <10> Novo Nordisk announced on January 31, 2024, that it would be progressively increasing the supply of its weight-loss medication, Wegovy, in the United States throughout the year to address significant demand. [7, 9] The company stated that it had already more than doubled the availability of the initial lower doses of the drug starting in January 2024. [2] The announcement was made during their fourth-quarter 2023 earnings call, where they also outlined plans for continued growth in 2024. [1, 5] Despite these efforts to ramp up production, the company acknowledged that demand would likely continue to surpass supply for some time. [2] By May 2024, Novo Nordisk reported it had quadrupled the supply of starter doses in the U.S. compared to the end of the previous year. [4]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On February 4, 2025, Epic Research published a report analyzing BMI trends in the United States using data from over 109 million patients between the first quarter of 2010 and the third quarter of 2024. [1, 2] In contrast, the overall obesity rate (BMI of 30 or greater) has remained largely unchanged since 2020, though it had increased by 13.6% between 2010 and 2024. [1, 2] The report also highlighted differing trends among age groups; adults aged 18 to 39 saw the most significant rise in median BMI, while the median BMI for adults aged 60 to 75 remained stable and even decreased in recent years. [1, 2] <2> The European Shortages Monitoring Platform (ESMP) became fully operational with its complete set of functionalities in late January 2025, with mandatory use for marketing authorisation holders and national competent authorities starting on February 2, 2025. [2, 4, 5] The European Medicines Agency (EMA) announced the platform's full launch on January 29, 2025, marking a key step in enhancing the monitoring and management of medication shortages across the European Union, including for high-demand GLP-1 receptor agonists used in treating obesity and diabetes. [9, 13] The study, which involved 150 children and their parents, demonstrated that the self-guided approach yielded similar weight loss results while being significantly more accessible and affordable. [3, 4] Instead, the commission proposes a more comprehensive set of 18 diagnostic criteria for adults and 13 for children and adolescents. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A multinational study published in PLOS Global Public Health on or around July 27, 2025, raised significant concerns over a proposed new definition for obesity. The research, a collaboration between scientists at Emory University, Johns Hopkins University, the University of Queensland, Zhejiang University, and two Peruvian universities, analyzed health data from 142,250 adults across 56 countries. The study evaluated a new criteria for clinical obesity that would require an individual to have a high BMI plus at least one existing health condition, such as diabetes, hypertension, or high cholesterol. The findings showed that adopting this definition would cause a dramatic decrease in obesity prevalence, with some nations seeing a drop of over 50%. However, the researchers urged caution, warning that this shift could impede the prevention and early detection of serious health issues. They argued it could provide a dangerous false sense of security for at-risk individuals no longer classified as obese, reduce the sensitivity of public health surveillance, delay diagnoses, and worsen inequities in healthcare access. <2> A study published in JAMA Network Open indicates a significant rise in severe obesity among children in the United States over a 15-year period. Research analyzing national health data from 2008 to 2023 found that overall obesity prevalence in children aged 2-19 increased from 19.46% to 22.52%. The study highlighted a particularly alarming trend in the most severe categories of obesity, with a 253% relative increase in "extremely severe obesity" for children between the ages of 2 and 18. Factors contributing to this public health issue include reduced physical activity, increased screen time, and a diet of high-calorie, low-nutrient foods, with the COVID-19 pandemic noted as an intensifying period. The rise in severe pediatric obesity increases the risk of serious health complications such as type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular disease. <3> An international study published in the journal PNAS, titled 'Energy expenditure and obesity across the economic spectrum', concludes that diet is a more significant driver of obesity than physical activity levels. [3, 8, 9] The research, co-authored by a global team including Eric Rimm from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and led by investigators including Amanda McGrosky and Herman Pontzer, analyzed data from over 4,200 adults across 34 diverse populations, from hunter-gatherers to individuals in industrialized nations. [2, 3, 8, 9] The study found that daily energy expenditure was surprisingly similar across different lifestyles and even slightly greater in developed populations, challenging the hypothesis that a lack of exercise is the primary cause of rising obesity rates. [3, 9] The findings suggest that increased caloric intake, particularly from ultra-processed foods, plays a much larger role in the higher prevalence of obesity in developed countries. [3, 9] While emphasizing the crucial health benefits of physical activity, the authors conclude that both diet and exercise should be viewed as essential and complementary, not interchangeable, public health priorities. [3, 8] <4> On July 8, 2025, the Obesity Action Coalition (OAC) and other health organizations, including the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, applauded the introduction of the bipartisan Treat and Reduce Obesity Act (H.R. 4231/S. 1973) in the U.S. Congress.
